nodes.name: Schrödinger equation with critical potential
nodes.statement:
This note is concerned with smoothing properties of the time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation
\begin{align} i\partial_t u(t,x)=Hu(t,x)+F(t,x);\quad u(0,x)=\psi(x),
\end{align}
with given data $\psi\in L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ and $F\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}};L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n))$, where $H=-\Delta+V(x)$ is a Schr\"odinger operator  on ${\mathbb{R}}^n$, $n\ge3$, with a real-valued function $V$ which decays at spatial infinity in a suitable sense and  has a critical singularity at the origin.
nodes.statement_short: The Cauchy problem (1.1) for $H=-\Delta+V$ on $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge3$, with $V$ decaying and critically singular at 0.

nodes.name: Kato–Yajima estimate from Hölder and endpoint Strichartz
nodes.statement:
The estimate \eqref{intro_2} also follows from H\"older's inequality and the endpoint Strichartz estimate proved by Keel and Tao \cite{KeTa}: 
\begin{align} \norm{e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}};L^{\frac{2n}{n-2}}({\mathbb{R}}^n))}\le C\norm{\psi}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)},
\end{align}
which can be also regarded as a smoothing property in $L^p$-spaces.
nodes.statement_short: Hölder's inequality applied to the Keel–Tao endpoint Strichartz estimate.

nodes.name: Inverse-square potential operator $H_a$
nodes.statement:
In particular, the Schr\"odinger operator with the inverse-square potential of the form\
$$
H_a=-\Delta+a|x|^{-2},\quad a>-\frac{(n-2)^2}{4},
$$
has attracted increasing attention since it represents a borderline case  for the validity of \eqref{intro_1}--\eqref{intro_3} (\cite{Duy,GVV}), where note that $(n-2)^2/4$ is the best constant in Hardy's inequality
\begin{align} \frac{(n-2)^2}{4}\int |x|^{-2}|u|^2dx\le \int|\nabla u|^2dx,\quad u\in C_0^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n). 
\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $H_a=-\Delta+a|x|^{-2}$, $a>-(n-2)^2/4$, a borderline case; $(n-2)^2/4$ is the Hardy constant.

nodes.name: Hardy's inequality
nodes.statement: \frac{(n-2)^2}{4}\int |x|^{-2}|u|^2dx\le \int|\nabla u|^2dx,\quad u\in C_0^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n).
nodes.label: Hardy

nodes.name: Smoothing estimate for inverse-square potentials (Bui–D'Ancona–Duong–Li–Ly)

nodes.name: Inverse-square potential satisfies Assumption A
nodes.statement: A typical example satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption_A} is the inverse-square potential $V(x)=a|x|^{-2}$ with $a>-(n-2)^2/4$. In this case, it follows from Hardy's inequality \eqref{Hardy} that \eqref{assumption_A_1} is satisfied with $\delta=1-4|a|/(n-2)^2>0$ if $a<0$ or $\delta=1$ if $a\ge0$.

nodes.name: Potentials with $|x|^2V\notin L^\infty$ satisfying Assumption A
nodes.statement:
Moreover, Assumption \ref{assumption_A} is general enough to include some potentials such that $|x|^2V\notin L^\infty$. For instance, we let $c_1,c_2>0$, $\alpha\in{\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $\chi\in C^1({\mathbb{R}})$ such that $0\le \chi\le 1$ and $|\chi^{(k)}(t)|\le |t|^{-k-1}$ for $|t|\ge1$. Then 
$$
V(x)=\frac{-(n-2)^2/4+c_1}{|x|^{2}}-\frac{c_2\chi(|x-\alpha|)}{|x-\alpha|}
$$
satisfies Assumption \ref{assumption_A} with $\delta=c_1-c_2(2+\sup|\chi'|)(|\alpha|+1)$ if 
$$
0<c_2<\frac{c_1}{(2+\sup|\chi'|)(|\alpha|+1)}. 
$$
nodes.statement_short: Inverse-square plus a Coulomb-type singularity at $\alpha$ satisfies Assumption A for small $c_2$.

nodes.name: Closability of the form $Q_H$
nodes.statement:
Under Assumption \ref{assumption_A}, Hardy's inequality \eqref{Hardy} implies that the sesquilinear form $$Q_H(u,v)=\<(-\Delta+V)u,v\>
,\quad u,v\in C_0^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n),$$ is symmetric, non-negative and closable such that the domain of its closure $\overline{Q}_H$ satisfies $D(\overline{Q}_H)=\mathcal H^1({\mathbb{R}}^n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Under Assumption A, $Q_H$ is symmetric, non-negative and closable with form domain $\mathcal H^1$.

nodes.name: Muckenhoupt $A_2$ class
nodes.statement:
We say that $v(x)$ belongs to the Muckenhoupt $A_2$ class if $v,1/v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}({\mathbb{R}}^n)$, $v\ge0$ and
$$

nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal{H}}$ be a Hilbert space with inner product $\<\cdot,\cdot\>$ and norm $\norm{\cdot}$, $H$ a self-adjoint operator on ${\mathcal{H}}$ and $A$ a densely defined closed operator on ${\mathcal{H}}$.

nodes.name: Resolvent $R_H(z)$
nodes.statement: Let $R_H(z):=(H-z)^{-1}$, $z\notin\sigma(H)$.

nodes.name: $H$-smooth operator (Kato)
nodes.statement:
Then we say that $A$ is {\it $H$-smooth} with bound $a$ if 
$$
\sup_{z\in {\mathbb{C}}\setminus{\mathbb{R}}}|\<(R_H(z)-R_H(\overline z))A^*\psi,A^*\psi\>|\le \frac{a^2}{2}\norm{\psi}^2,\quad \psi\in D(A^*). 
$$
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is $H$-smooth with bound $a$ if $\sup_z|\langle(R_H(z)-R_H(\bar z))A^*\psi,A^*\psi\rangle|\le a^2\|\psi\|^2/2$.

nodes.name: $H$-supersmooth operator
nodes.statement:
We say that $A$ is {\it $H$-supersmooth} with bound $a$ if 
$$
\sup_{z\in {\mathbb{C}}\setminus{\mathbb{R}}}|\<R_H(z)A^*\psi,A^*\psi\>|\le \frac{a}{2}\norm{\psi}^2,\quad \psi\in D(A^*). 
$$
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is $H$-supersmooth with bound $a$ if $\sup_z|\langle R_H(z)A^*\psi,A^*\psi\rangle|\le a\|\psi\|^2/2$.

nodes.name: Supersmoothness implies smoothness
nodes.statement: Note that if $A$ is $H$-supersmooth with bound $a$ then $A$ is $H$-smooth with bound $(2a)^{1/2}$.

nodes.statement:

$$

nodes.label: adjoint_1

nodes.name: $\Gamma_H^*$ is the adjoint of $\Gamma_H$
nodes.statement:
By a direct calculation, $\<\<\Gamma_HF,G\>\>_T=\<\<F,\Gamma_H^*G\>\>_T$ for $F,G\in L^1_{\mathop{\mathrm{loc}}\nolimits}{\mathcal{H}}$, where 
$$
\<\<F,G\>\>_T:=\int_{-T}^T\<F(t),G(t)\>dt. 
$$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement:
For the sake of self-containedness, we give the proof for $\Gamma_H$ in detail. The proof for $\Gamma_H^*$ is analogous. Let $\chi\in C_0^\infty({\mathbb{R}})$ be such that $\chi\equiv1$ near $0$ and $0\le\chi\le1$ and set $\chi_{\varepsilon}(t)=\chi({\varepsilon} t)$. Note that $A\Gamma_H\chi_{\varepsilon}(H)=A\chi_{\varepsilon}(H)\Gamma_H$ is well-defined on $L^1_T{\mathcal{H}}$ since $A$ is $H$-bounded. Moreover, the $H$-smoothness of $A$ shows$$ ignorm{Ae^{-itH}\int_{[0,T]}e^{isH}\chi_{\varepsilon}(H)F(s)ds}_{L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}}\le a
orm{F}_{L^1_T{\mathcal{H}}}.$$Using the Christ-Kiselev lemma \cite{ChKi}, one can replace $[0,T]$ by $[0,t]$ in the left hand side to obtain$$
orm{A\chi_{\varepsilon}(H)\Gamma_HF}_{L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}}\le Ca
orm{F}_{L^1_T{\mathcal{H}}}$$with some universal constant $C>0$ independent of $F$. This estimate implies that, for all $F\in L^1_T{\mathcal{H}}$, $A\chi_{\varepsilon}(H)\Gamma_HF$ converges in $L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}$ as ${\varepsilon}	o0$ and the limit denoted by the same symbol $A\Gamma_HF$ satisfies the first estimate in \eqref{lemma_abstract_2_1}. This proves the half part of this lemma. Next, let $F:[-T,T]	o {\mathcal{H}}$ be a simple function. As we have shown, $A\chi_{{\varepsilon}_n}(H)\Gamma_H$ converges to $A\Gamma_HF$ in $L^2_T{\mathcal{H}}$ as $n	o\infty$ for any sequence ${\varepsilon}_n>0$ with ${\varepsilon}_n	o0$. Then one can find a subsequence ${\varepsilon}_{n_k}$ and a null set $\mathcal N\subset [-T,T]$ such that $A\chi_{{\varepsilon}_{n_k}}(H)\Gamma_HF	o A\Gamma_HF(t)$ in ${\mathcal{H}}$ as $k	o\infty$ for all $t\in [-T,T]\setminus \mathcal N$. Hence, in order to show \eqref{lemma_abstract_2_2}, it suffices to check that $$  ignorm{\int_0^tAe^{-i(t-s)H}F(s)ds-A\chi_{{\varepsilon}_{n_k}}(H)\Gamma_HF(t)}_{\mathcal{H}}	o0 $$ as $k	o\infty$ for all $t\in [-T,T]\setminus \mathcal N$. Let us write $F=\sum_{j=1}^N\mathds1_{E_j}(t)f_j$ with $f_j\in {\mathcal{H}}$ and measurable sets $E_j\subset [-T,T]$. Then we have for all $t\in [-T,T]\setminus \mathcal N$,  egin{align*} & ignorm{\int_0^tAe^{-i(t-s)H}F(s)ds-A\chi_{{\varepsilon}_{n_k}}(H)\Gamma_HF(t)}_{\mathcal{H}}\ &\le \sum_{j=1}^N ignorm{\int_{[0,t]\cap M_j}Ae^{isH}(1-\chi_{{\varepsilon}_{n_k}}(H))e^{-itH}f_jds}_{\mathcal{H}}\ &\le \sum_{j=1}^NT^{1/2}\Big(\int_{\mathbb{R}}
orm{Ae^{isH}e^{-itH}(1-\chi_{{\varepsilon}_{n_k}}(H))f_j}_{{\mathcal{H}}}^2ds\Big)^{1/2}\ &\le CT^{1/2}\sum_{j=1}^N

nodes.statement:
Let us first consider \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_1}. When $n=1$, it was proved by \cite{KPV}  that
$$
\sup_{x\in {\mathbb{R}}}\norm{|D_x|^{1/2}e^{it\partial_x^2}f}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}_t)}\le C \norm{f}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}}_x)}
$$
which, together with the unitarity of $e^{it\Delta_{\widehat{x}_j}}$ in $L^2({\mathbb{R}}^{n-1})$, implies
$$
\norm{|D_j|^{1/2} e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^\infty_{x_j}L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_j}}
\le C\norm{\psi}_{L^2},\quad j=1,2,...,n,
$$
uniformly in $T>0$, where $\widehat x_j=(x_1,...,x_{j-1},x_{j+1},...,x_n)\in {\mathbb{R}}^{n-1}$ and $D_j=-i\partial_{x_j}$. \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_1} then is derived from this estimate as follows. Let $\{C_j(\xi)\}$ be a conical partition of unity on ${\mathbb{R}}^n$ so that $
I=\sum_{j=1}^n C_j(\xi),
$
where $C_j\in C^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^n\setminus\{0\})$ such that $\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\nolimits C_j\subset\{2|\xi_j|>|\xi|\}$ and $\partial_\xi^\alpha C_j(\xi)=O(|\xi|^{-|\alpha|})$. If we set 
$
\wtilde C_j(\xi)=C_j(\xi)|\xi|^{1/2}|\xi_j|^{-1/2}
$ then $\wtilde C_j$ also satisfies $\partial_\xi^\alpha C_j(\xi)=O(|\xi|^{-|\alpha|})$ and
$
|\xi|^{1/2}=\sum_{j=1}^n\wtilde C_j(\xi)|\xi_j|^{1/2}. 
$
Since $w(|x|)^2$ belongs to the Muckenhoupt $A_2$-class, $\wtilde C_j(D)$ is bounded on a weighted space $L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n,w(|x|)^2dx)$ by weighted Mikhlin's multiplier theorem (see \cite{KuWh}). Thus we conclude that
\begin{align*}
\norm{w(|x|)|D|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^2_TL^2}^2
&\le \sum_{j=1}^n\norm{w(|x|)\wtilde C_j(D)|D_{j}|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^2_TL^2}^2\\
&\le C\sum_{j=1}^n\norm{w(|x|)|D_{j}|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^2_TL^2}^2\\

&\le C\sum_{j=1}^n\norm{w}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}})}^2\norm{|D_{j}|^{1/2}e^{it\Delta}\psi}_{L^\infty_{x_j}L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_j}}^2\\
&\le C \norm{w}_{L^2({\mathbb{R}})}^2\norm{\psi}_{L^2}^2
\end{align*}
uniformly in $T>0$, where we used the properties $w(|x|)\le C_jw(x_j)$ and $w\in L^2({\mathbb{R}})$ in the third line.

nodes.name: Proof of (3.6)
nodes.statement:
Next, by the same argument as above, \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_2} follows from the following estimate
\begin{align*}
\norm{|D_j|^{1/2}\Gamma_0 F}_{L^\infty_{x_j}L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_j}}
\le C \norm{F}_{L^2_TL^{2_*,2}}.
\end{align*}
which is a slight generalization of \cite[Lemma 4]{IoKe}, in which the same estimate with $L^{2_*,2}$ replaced by $L^{2_*}$ was proved. Although the proof is essentially same as that of \cite[Lemma 4]{IoKe}, we briefly recall its strategy for reader's convenience. Without loss of generality, we may assume $j=1$. Then it suffices to show 
\begin{align} \sup_{x_1}\norm{|D_j|^{1/2}\wtilde\Gamma_0 F}_{L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_1}}\le C\norm{F}_{L^2_TL^{2_*,2}},
\end{align}
where $\wtilde \Gamma_0 $ is defined by
$$
\wtilde \Gamma_0 F(t):=\int_{-\infty}^te^{i(t-s)\Delta}F(s)ds.
$$
Indeed, the corresponding estimate for $\Gamma_0 -\wtilde\Gamma_0 $ follows from \eqref{lemma_smoothing_2_1} and the dual estimate of \eqref{lemma_proof_1_1}. The only difference from the proof of \cite[Lemma 4]{IoKe} is an interpolation step. While they used the complex interpolation, we will use a real interpolation technique as in \cite[Section 6]{KeTa}. Let $I_{\pm}=\mathbf1_{\pm}(D_1)|D_1|^{1/2}\wtilde\Gamma_0 $, where $\mathbf 1_\pm(t)=1$ for $\pm t\ge0$ and $\mathbf 1_\pm(t)=0$ for $\mp t\ge0$. 
It suffices to show that $I_{+}$ is bounded from $L^2_TL^{2_*,2}$ to $L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_1}$ uniformly in $x_1$ since the proof for $I_{-}$ being analogous. By the $TT^*$ argument, $I_{+}\in \mathbb B(L^2_TL^{2_*,2},L^2_TL^2_{\widehat x_1})$ if $I_{+}^*I_{+}$ is bounded from $L^2_TL^{2_*,2}$ to $L^2_TL^{2^*,2}$. Hence, if we define a bilinear form $I$ by$$
I(F,G):=\iint \<I_{+}F(s,\cdot),I_{+}G(t,\cdot)\>dsdt
$$
then it suffices to show that 
\begin{align} |I(F,G)|\le C\norm{F}_{L^2_TL^{2_*,2}}\norm{G}_{L^2_TL^{2_*,2}}
\end{align}
uniformly in $x_1$ and $T>0$. It was shown by \cite{IoKe} that $I_{+}^*I_{+}$ is bounded on $L^2({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ and the kernel of $I_{+}^*I_{+}$, denoted by $K_{+}(t,s,x,y)$, satisfies the dispersive estimate:
$$
|K_{+}(t,s,x,y)|\le C|t-s|^{-n/2},\quad t\neq s.
$$
We then decompose $I(F,G)$ as
$$
I(F,G)=\sum_{k\in{\mathbb{Z}}}I_k(F,G),\ I_k(F,G):=\iint_{t-2^{k+1}}^{t-2^k} \<I_{+}F(s,\cdot),I_{+}G(t,\cdot)\>dsdt. 
$$
By using the same argument as in \cite[Lemma 4.1]{KeTa}, we see that 
\begin{align*}
|I_k(F,G)|\le  C2^{-k\beta(a,b)}\norm{F}_{L^2_TL^{a'}}\norm{G}_{L^2_TL^{b'}},\quad \beta(a,b)=\frac n2-1-\frac n2(\frac1a-\frac1b)
\end{align*}
uniformly in $k\in {\mathbb{Z}}$, where $(a,b)$ satisfies one of the following conditions:
$$
\text{(i)\ \ $\frac 1a=\frac 1b=0$;\quad (ii)\ \ $\frac{n-1}{2n}\le \frac1a \le \frac12$ and $\frac 1b=\frac12$;\quad (iii)\ \ $\frac{n-1}{2n}\le \frac1b \le \frac12$ and $\frac 1a=\frac12$. }
$$
In other words, a vector valued sequence $(I_k)_{k\in {\mathbb{Z}}}$ is bounded from $L^2_TL^{a'}_x\times L^2_TL^{b'}_x$ to $\ell_{\beta(a,b)}^\infty$, where $\ell^p_s=L^p({\mathbb{Z}}, 2^{js}dj)$ is a weighted $\ell^p$ space with the counting measure $dj$. Then \eqref{lemma_magnetic_1_3} follows from the technique by \cite[Section 6]{KeTa} based on a bilinear real interpolation.
